Since I had initialized the NexJS app already, it detected that there was code present and asked if it should explore the existing codebase first. We told it to skip the mapping to avoid wasting time. If you were working on an existing project, it would be better to ask it to map the codebase first, but since it contained the blank template, I skipped it. After that, it will ask you to tell it the app idea you want to work on. After which, it asks a lot of questions regarding the target audience of your app, its features, the scope of the project, and more. But the question answer session GSD conducts is noticeably different from that of the superpowers. Superpowers try to extract edge cases from you during this phase. GSD does not, and it focuses more on understanding what to build, not stress testing how it might break. Once it gathers enough information from the session, it creates the project.md inside the dotplanning folder which contains the description out of scope items, context constraints, and key decisions all deduced from the questioning. But here's where the context rot prevention shows up in practice. It keeps project.md deliberately short and focused so the agents wouldn't deviate from the main aims by getting buried in documentation. It tracks all the work through git, but it doesn't use a straightforward git commit. It runs a script underneath that performs checks before committing, ensuring everything is up to the standards before actually using git to commit. Once planning was done, GSD moved to the research phase. It spawns multiple agents researching different aspects of the app in parallel, all running in the background. After the research completes, the research synthesizer agent kicks in. Since all these agents are tuned to use appropriate models for the tasks, the synthesizer agent uses the sonnet model, not the heavier opus. GSD has a proper reference mapping each sub aent to the right model based on the weight of work it handles so that it doesn't waste extra efforts. It condenses the research findings and also flagged potential issues. Things to watch out for that could hinder the work long-term. After the research is synthesized, the requirement stage begins. It asks you targeted questions about the MVP, identifying which features are truly essential for version one. Because GSD is focused on fast delivery, it makes sure V1 contains only what is necessary. After it confirms the MVP with you, it then generates the road map structure which you have to approve. And your approval marks the project initialization as complete. Also, if you are enjoying our content, consider pressing the hype button because it helps us create more content like this and reach out to more people. Now [snorts] that the initialization phase is over, the next step is to implement the plan. In the previous phase, it had broken the project down into four phases based on the requirement. It will give you two ways to work. either skip discussions or proceed with discussions. Discussion for this framework means questioning sessions with the agent where it ensures it understands the plan properly. We chose to discuss first so that we can clarify the requirements as much as we can. But you can choose to skip discussions if you think the previous questioning session was enough for it to build the app. Once the discussion session is over, it creates a context.md file in the phases folder inside the planning folder. This file contains all the details of what we have discussed and map the phase we just talked about with the agent. But true to GSD's philosophy, this file is also concise in length so that Claude can stay focused on what actually matters. Next, you begin the planning of phase one. The planning phase starts with the research based on the context.md file it just created using a dedicated research agent with the set model exploring different aspects. But we thought it would use context 7 or actually look up against the docs properly. Instead, it was using web search with the year 2025 in the search keywords, which it shouldn't have been doing. It would have been more controlled if we had connected context 7 MCP so that its research was better grounded. So, when you are using, make sure to connect with such MCP for better grounding. It created a research.md file and documented all of its research including the confidence level for its research, which indicated how trustworthy are its sources. After the research, it created a plan. These plans listed in detail the dependencies of each phase and all the requirements with proper IDs. But here's the thing. This is where GSD is different because instead of just writing the plan one way like others do, it actually cross-verifies the plan across multiple dimensions and validates whether the plan is actually implementable and aligned with the goals. It uses dedicated planning and verifying plan agents where the planning agent creates the plans and the verifier keeps checking them sending warnings back. So it basically performs the adversarial planning on its own without us having to control any of that manually. Once the plan was final and all the steps had passed, it committed and broke the plan down into two waves. It actually breaks down into as many waves as required and parallelizes those that are independent so that sub agents can handle them in parallel. It started implementing the project waves using the dedicated agent to carry out the plan it created. Once it is finished, it verifies the checkpoint using proper playright testing underneath, creating scripts, deleting them after using to clean the folder, and performing multiple automated tasks under the hood. It then gave us a summary of what was built and provided instructions on how to verify it for ourselves. The first iteration builds the app that is just a placeholder with all the initial elements visible to show how the app would actually look. Further iterations will build one aspect of the app at a time, leading to a complete app at the end of the cycle. The entire iteration used 138,000 tokens, which was actually not much given a 1 million token context window. But with an agent with a 200,000 context window, it would signal that it's time to compact. But since this relies on documentation of phases, even if we clear the context, the agents would know where to start. When we approved the work, it ran multiple tests and marked wave 2 as complete as well. After that, it spawned the GSD verifier again and cross-cheed whether the implementation actually matched the initial goal. Once verified, it marked phase one as complete, including the verifications, and prompted us to proceed to the next phase of the application. Now, once we ran the app through all of the phases, the previously placeholder features were all functional and working as intended. GST works well when you're working on a large-scale application with multiple features, but it's overkill if the app you're building is much simpler and doesn't need the heavy lifting. For simpler apps, Claude or any other agent on its own is sufficient and doesn't need this thorough planning. However, if you want controlled execution with proper planning without wasting too much effort on this phase, you should definitely go for GSD. Now, this is one framework, but often times there are use cases where the existing ones don't hold up and you need to build one of your own. For that, you need to know certain principles before actually building your own. We covered those principles in a previous video that would help you build better workflows. You might end up seeing that video on the end screen, so you can just click on it instead of looking it up. [snorts] That brings us to the end of this video. If you'd like to support the channel and help us keep making videos like this, you can do so by joining AIAS Pro. As always, thank you for watching and I'll see you in the next one.

Every AI coding agent framework claims to be the best. GSD, get shit done, is built different. Whether you use Claude Code, Gemini CLI, or any vibe coding setup, picking the wrong framework with Claude wastes more time than bad code.

SuperPowers Video: https://youtu.be/romGzY0Xu0s?si=QQqBx2DKNANSHz0V 
Get Shit Done: https://github.com/gsd-build/get-shit-done

AI agents framework selection is the real bottleneck, not the framework itself. In this video, we break down three approaches, GSD, BMAD, and Superpowers, and show you exactly when to use each one. GSD is built for experimental MVPs where requirements shift, BMAD is for locked-in specs with thorough pre-planning, and Superpowers uses TDD for high-stakes agentic AI systems where edge cases can't be missed.

We walk through a full GSD installation and build, from the initial planning phase through multi-wave implementation with subagents, adversarial plan verification, and Playwright testing. You'll see how it manages context rot, parallelizes work across coding agents, and keeps documentation concise so your AI automation pipeline stays focused.

Whether you're evaluating the best AI for coding your next MVP or comparing the best coding AI workflows for production apps, this breakdown will help you stop guessing. Most coding AI comparisons skip the selection criteria entirely, they just tell you which AI tools are trending. We go deeper into how AI works within each framework and why the structure around your AI matters more than the model itself. If you've looked at OpenAI, Claude, or any other provider and wondered why your agent keeps drifting off task, the answer is usually in the framework, not the model.

This applies whether you're using Claude Code, vibe coding solo projects, or building with opencode alternatives. The principles carry across every coding setup. And if none of the existing frameworks fit, we point you to a previous video on bu
